evidence: src/domain/shared/Money.ts: the private constructor plus the static ofCents(cents) factory hold the single non-negative-integer-cents invariant (`!Number.isInteger(cents) || cents < 0`).
src/domain/shared/Money.ts: multiply(factor) calls Money.ofCents(this.cents * factor), so a result that could be invalid is re-checked by the module's own factory.
src/domain/shared/Money.ts: add() and zero() use the constructor directly, which is safe because the result always meets the invariant.

src/domain/shared/Quantity.ts: the private constructor plus the static of(value) factory hold the single positive-integer invariant (`!Number.isInteger(value) || value <= 0`). add() keeps it, since adding two positive integers gives a positive integer.
Both files report broken invariants with the same ValidationError from ../errors/DomainErrors, so error handling is consistent.
The graph shows both classes used together by OrderLine, Order and Product, which supports their placement in a single shared value-object module.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Both files hold the same kind of thing: small immutable domain value objects that several bounded contexts share (order, product, inventory). Each class follows the same pattern: a private constructor, a validating static factory (Money.ofCents, Quantity.of) that throws ValidationError, and closed arithmetic.

Each class enforces its own invariant in exactly one place. Money must be a non-negative integer number of cents, checked in ofCents. Quantity must be a positive integer, checked in of. The two invariants differ, so neither copies the other.

Money.add, Money.zero and Quantity.add call the private constructor directly. That is safe, because adding two valid values (and creating zero) always yields a valid value. Money.multiply, whose result could break the invariant, goes back through the validating factory ofCents. So neither file goes around its own abstractions.

No unrelated concerns are mixed in.
